root.note: The TLFi says Arabic sukkar, Greek sákkharon and Latin saccharum all go back to this Indian word.

history: Sucre travelled from India to France through Arabic and Italian. Its oldest known ancestor is the Sanskrit word śarkarā; the TLFi notes that Arabic sukkar, Greek sákkharon and Latin saccharum all share this Indian origin. The Arabs brought the growing of sugar cane to Andalusia and Sicily, and Italian took their word as zucchero. French borrowed it from Italian. Chrétien de Troyes writes çucre in his Chevalier au lion, around 1176–81, and the spelling sucre is found at the end of the 13th century. In the kitchen French distinguishes le sucre en poudre, ‘caster sugar’, from le sucre en morceaux, ‘sugar cubes’. The adjective is sucré, ‘sweet’, and its opposite, for food, is salé.
historyEinfach: Sucre comes from a very old Indian word, śarkarā. The Arabs said sukkar. They grew sugar cane in Spain and Sicily. Italian took the word: zucchero. Then French took it from Italian. Sucré means ‘sweet’: le café sucré.

elsewhere.text: Italian was the last stop before French. The z of zucchero shows in the old French spellings çucre and zucre.
